content: The Continuous Quality Improvement (CQI) process at the provider level involves various elements such as job aids, supportive supervision, follow-up training, and mentorship. At the facility level, CQI may include actions like small infrastructure modifications, changes to admission procedures, or improved signage to enhance privacy and confidentiality for adolescent clients. Informational materials and visual aids can assist providers in effectively communicating with adolescents living with HIV (ALHIV) about their treatment and care needs. Ensuring the availability of necessary equipment and supplies supports the timely and appropriate delivery of services. The involvement of peer educators and lay health workers can help reduce the workload of healthcare workers while providing additional support. Negative attitudes from healthcare workers disproportionately affect adolescents compared to adults, with an even greater impact on young people from key populations. Healthcare providers must develop skills to listen attentively, communicate clearly, and recognize the hesitancy and discomfort adolescents may feel when discussing their concerns. Training may be required to help providers deliver such care effectively. Training healthcare workers on HIV-related services for adolescents is urgently needed, particularly in integrating adolescent-specific content into existing HIV training for adults or incorporating HIV-related content into adolescent health training. Pre-service training on adolescent health, ALHIV, adolescent sexual and reproductive health, and young key populations is also essential. Social workers play a critical role in supporting ALHIV, and their involvement should be considered when planning to strengthen human resources. Adolescents should be supported in disclosing their status to others for emotional support and to sexual partners for safer sex practices, while prioritizing adherence to treatment and consistent condom use. Adolescents should also receive guidance on family planning, including decisions about having children and planning for their future education and employment. Training healthcare workers involves not only knowledge transfer but also attitude and behavior change, which requires ongoing supervision and professional support. While evidence supporting community-based interventions and health worker training for treatment adherence and retention in care is limited, these interventions are considered important and warrant further research. Recommendations for these interventions are based on the best judgment of practitioners and advocates. The World Health Organization (WHO) consolidated guidelines on antiretroviral drug use for HIV treatment and prevention include several service delivery recommendations. These include community-based HIV testing and counseling (HTC) with linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services, particularly for key populations. Integration of HIV services into maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) settings and tuberculosis (TB) treatment settings is recommended, as is decentralization of antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation and maintenance to peripheral health facilities or community-based organizations. Task-shifting, where trained non-physician clinicians, midwives, and nurses initiate and maintain ART, is also recommended. Mobile phone text messages may be used as a tool to promote ART adherence. Adolescents require tailored approaches to HIV testing and care. Community-based HTC is particularly important for older adolescents who may have been horizontally infected, as this group is often under-tested. Post-test counseling, service linkage, and confidentiality are critical concerns for adolescents. Integration of HIV services with TB, antenatal care (ANC), and services for injecting drug users (IDU) should address the specific needs of adolescents, such as early enrollment in ANC for pregnant adolescents and support throughout pregnancy, including ART adherence and safe infant feeding choices. National plans should explicitly include adolescents, particularly those from key populations. Decentralizing HIV treatment and care to locations closer to adolescents' homes can improve access. Strong linkages with NGOs and community groups working with adolescents and ALHIV are essential. Mobile technologies, familiar to adolescents, can support adherence and social support for people living with HIV (PLHIV). Guiding principles for designing and implementing HTC and care services for adolescents include voluntary testing, recognizing the heterogeneity of adolescents, meaningful involvement of adolescents in program development, and ensuring confidentiality. Services must be developmentally appropriate and consider the evolving capacity of adolescents. A supportive legal and policy environment is critical for adolescents to access and benefit from HIV-related services. Legal protections are necessary for adolescents who experience sexual exploitation or violence, with referrals to appropriate child protection services. Expanding access to HTC and improving the quality of health services for ALHIV are priorities. The UNICEF ALHIV Lessons Learned project aims to provide practical examples to guide accelerated action in meeting the needs of ALHIV. In South Africa, adolescents aged 12 and older can consent to HIV testing if they are deemed mature enough to understand the implications. This policy reflects efforts to support adolescents' autonomy and access to healthcare. Linking HIV testing with prevention, treatment, and care is essential, particularly for vulnerable adolescents. Group counseling programs, such as the Hlanganani program in South Africa, have shown promise in supporting newly diagnosed adolescents to link to care and commence ART when eligible. These programs may also be adapted for adolescents transitioning into adult care.
